critique.good: The numeric headers share a two-line rhythm, and the tier names and percentages remain intact.

critique.cause: The 110px uptime column leaves 89px for text, too little to combine its header words on two lines. The 90px credit column leaves enough room for each header word.

critique.good: The service credit header fits on one line, and the tier names, values, and support terms remain intact. The body retains a clear comparison structure.
critique.problems: The single-line credit header does not reduce the header height because the uptime header still takes three lines. The support column is narrower without a visible reduction in row height.
critique.cause: The 109px credit column uses 19px more than in r2A, while the 101px uptime column still forces a three-line header and the support column falls to 272px.

understanding.purpose: Compare SLA tiers by their uptime commitments, service credits, and support channels.
understanding.reading: Readers scan down the tier names, compare uptime and credit values across tiers, and read across each row to see the support included.
groups: Monthly uptime commitment and service credit are compact, comparable numeric terms of the SLA.
Support channels is descriptive text associated with each tier and needs the most room for natural wrapping.
keep_intact: Uptime percentages and service credit percentages
may_wrap: Monthly uptime commitment and Service credit headers
Support channels descriptions at spaces or between listed channels
Header wrapping can use height shared across the header row; support text can use height shared across each data row.

bad.why: The wide uptime column leaves the support descriptions cramped. The professional and mission-critical rows become disproportionately tall, with the professional description broken into four lines.

final.rationale: r2B gives the support descriptions enough width to fit each tier in at most two lines, making the three body rows easy to compare. The tier names and service-credit header remain intact, while the three-line uptime header occupies space only once. The resulting body has a steady rhythm without spending excessive width on short percentages.

general: Allocate width according to content and scanning needs, rather than making columns equal by default.
A taller header can be a worthwhile trade for clearer, more consistent body rows.
Keep row identifiers and meaningful words intact where possible.
specific: Support channels carry most of this table's text and benefit most from the extra width.
The two percentage columns contain short values, so they can remain relatively narrow.

final.tradeoffs: r1B keeps the uptime header to two lines and the service-credit header to one, but its professional support description takes three lines. r2B uses a three-line uptime header to make both longer support descriptions two lines.
final.uncertain: A designer could prefer the shorter header in r1B or the wider uptime column in r2A. The ranges are conservative visual estimates for small adjustments, with the other columns scaled proportionally; their exact limits would need browser verification.

A.why: Row labels stay intact, but the wide uptime column leaves the support text cramped, producing several short lines in the longer entries.

B.why: The generous support column makes the long entries easy to read, but the uptime header is squeezed into three lines.

C.why: Support text has reasonable space, but the Mission-critical row label breaks across lines, weakening the row header.

D.why: The support column is too narrow for the descriptive content, causing extensive wrapping and tall rows while the percentage columns have excess space.

E.why: Row labels remain intact and the columns are balanced, though both percentage headers wrap and the longer support entries need several lines.

F.why: The row labels remain intact, the service credit header fits on one line, and the support column has enough room for readable phrases. The columns have a clear, balanced rhythm.

reviews.unsure: B is also a strong option if shorter support entries are valued more than a compact header.

A.why: Tier names remain intact, and the numerical columns are easy to scan. Both numerical headers wrap, while the longer support entries use two or three lines.

B.why: All tier names stay intact, service credit fits on one line, and the generous support column keeps its entries to two lines. The uptime header takes three lines, but remains clear.

C.why: The wide uptime column leaves little room for support channels, producing tall, fragmented entries and uneven use of space.

D.why: The support column reads comfortably, but Mission-critical breaks across lines and the service credit header also wraps.

E.why: Tier names and the service credit header stay intact, and the support text has enough room to read comfortably. The two-line uptime header balances the columns well.

F.why: Oversized numeric columns squeeze support channels into a narrow strip, breaking even the shortest entry and making the longer entries difficult to scan.

reviews.unsure: B gives support descriptions more space, while E gives the uptime header a more compact shape; the preference between them is close.
